subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: Note from Usha, coach. In today's football game a quarrel started over whether the ball had crossed the line. Vishal made a T with his hands and called, “Time out! Can we check the rule?” Both teams paused. We looked at the rule together and the argument ended. Later, in a different game, another child made the T when his team was behind. His friends said, “You just want to stop because you're losing,” and he went red. I did not scold him. I asked him what he needed, and he said he was upset. We took a short break and he rejoined.

qa.q: What did Vishal ask the players to check when he made a T?
qa.a: He asked them to check the rule.

qa.q: What was the second child probably feeling when he made the T, and what did his friends assume?
qa.a: Probably upset about being behind, as he later told Usha. His friends assumed he wanted to stop because he was losing, which was partly true and partly missing his distress.

qa.q: What did Usha do that worked with the second child?
qa.a: She did not scold him and asked what he needed, so he could say he was upset, and a short break helped him rejoin.

qa.q: How might Vishal's teammates see his T compared with the second child's?
qa.a: They probably saw Vishal's as honest, since he wanted to check a rule, while the second child's looked like dodging a loss.

grounding: A T with the hands pauses a game or quarrel; used honestly it lowers conflict, but peers notice when it dodges a loss.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: Pankaj's diary, Sunday. Made a T with my hands today when Uma was about to win at Ludo. She said, “That's not fair. You always call time-out when you're behind!” I said I needed to check the rule about sixes, but honestly I wasn't sure. I felt hot in the face. I think she's partly right. I was scared to lose again. So I told her sorry and said we could keep playing. She said okay and then she won anyway, and it wasn't as bad as I thought. Next time I'll call time-out only when there really is a rule to clear up.

qa.q: Which game were Pankaj and Uma playing?
qa.a: They were playing Ludo.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he made the T, and what does he admit?
qa.a: He was scared of losing again and felt hot in the face. He admits Uma is partly right, even though he said it was about the rule.

qa.q: What could Pankaj try next time he feels upset in a game?
qa.a: Use the time-out only for real rule questions, and say plainly if he is upset and needs a moment.

qa.q: How might Uma feel when Pankaj apologises and keeps playing?
qa.a: Probably relieved, since her complaint was heard, and happy that the game goes on. She might also feel a little proud of winning.

grounding: A T with the hands pauses a game; using it to dodge a loss is noticed by peers, while honest use lowers conflict.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: The gilli-danda game behind the village temple had turned into shouting. “You're out!” “I'm not! It didn't touch the ground!” Nazia and two boys were nose to nose. Chaitanya, holding the danda, stepped into the middle and made a T with his hands, high above his head. “Time out! Time out!” Everyone stopped, panting. “We're fighting about the rule, not the game,” he said. “Let's ask Rafi Chacha. He's played for forty years.” They trooped to the tea stall. Rafi Chacha said the gilli has to touch the ground first. Nazia was not out. Chaitanya made the T again, then turned it into a thumbs-up. “Game on.”

qa.q: Who did they ask about the rule?
qa.a: They asked Rafi Chacha at the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he stepped into the middle?
qa.a: He was probably worried the shouting would turn into a real fight and wanted to calm everyone down.

qa.q: Why did the time-out work here?
qa.a: It paused the quarrel to clarify the rule with someone fair, so the game could restart without bad feelings.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel after the rule was checked?
qa.a: Nazia probably felt relieved and fairly treated, since the rule showed she was not out.

grounding: Shows a child using the time-out T honestly to pause a quarrel and clarify a rule, lowering conflict.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: Liam was losing at tag in the Auckland park, and he knew it. Wei was two steps behind him when Liam spun round and made a T with his hands. “Time out! Shoelace!” Wei stopped. Liam bent over his shoe, which was already tied, and caught his breath. Then he ran off again, laughing. Ten minutes later, cornered by the slide, he made the T again. “Time out! Stitch!” Wei folded his arms. “That's your second time out, and both times I nearly had you.” The others had noticed too. Liam's face went pink. “Okay,” he muttered. “No more. You got me.” He held out his arm for Wei to tag.

qa.q: Where did Wei corner Liam?
qa.a: Wei cornered Liam by the slide.

qa.q: What was Liam likely feeling when he made the T the second time?
qa.a: He was probably tired and embarrassed about losing, using the time-out to avoid being caught rather than for a real need.

qa.q: What made Wei's response fair?
qa.a: Wei calmly pointed out the pattern instead of shouting, which let Liam admit it and play on honestly.

qa.q: How did the other children see Liam's time-outs?
qa.a: They noticed too, so the dodge made Liam look less fair in the game.

grounding: Shows a child using the time-out gesture to dodge losing, and peers spotting it.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: In the practice match at the district football academy, Nilesh and a defender clashed heads going for the ball. Nilesh sat down hard and didn't get up. Play went on around him. Varun, his teammate, stopped dead, turned towards the coach's bench and made a big T with both hands. “Time out! Nilesh is hurt!” The coach blew the whistle at once and jogged over. Nilesh was holding his forehead, dazed. The coach knelt, checked his eyes, asked him a few questions, then sent him to the medical room with the assistant. Afterwards the coach found Varun. “Good call. That's exactly what the T is for.”

qa.q: Where did the coach send Nilesh?
qa.a: The coach sent Nilesh to the medical room with the assistant.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he stopped dead?
qa.a: Varun was worried and alarmed that Nilesh was hurt and that nobody had noticed.

qa.q: Why was Varun's time-out an honest use of the signal?
qa.a: It paused the game to get help for a real injury, which is exactly what the T is meant for.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have felt sitting dazed while play went on?
qa.a: Nilesh may have felt confused and alone until Varun's signal brought the coach over.

grounding: Shows a child using the time-out T to pause a game and get help, an honest use that keeps players safe.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage:
I'm Salma, Jatin's classmate, and I was on the other team in Friday's kho-kho match. Halfway through, Deepak and Vinod started shoving over whether a foul counted. Jatin ran between them and made a T with his hands, flat palm on top of his fingers. "Time out! Let's ask Sir." Everyone froze. Sir explained the rule, and we played on.

Later, Rinku was about to be tagged, and suddenly he made a T too. "Time out! My lace!" His laces were perfectly tied. Everybody groaned, and even his own team shouted, "Play!"

I don't know what Jatin was thinking, but his T stopped a fight, and Rinku's just stopped the game.

qa.q: What did Rinku say was the problem?
qa.a: His lace, though his laces were perfectly tied.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling when he ran between Deepak and Vinod?
qa.a: Probably worried that the shoving would turn into a real fight and keen to settle the rule fairly, though Salma can't know for sure.

qa.q: What made Jatin's time-out work where Rinku's failed?
qa.a: Jatin used it honestly to stop a quarrel and get help with a rule, while Rinku used it to dodge being tagged, and everyone could see his laces were tied.

qa.q: How did the other players see Rinku's time-out?
qa.a: They saw through it and felt annoyed, groaning and shouting "Play!", even his own team.

grounding: It is a classmate's account of one child using the time-out T honestly to stop a quarrel and another using it to dodge being tagged, which peers spot.
